title: Remember a good person
hookLine: keep someone who lived virtuously in mind (Meditations 11.26)

cards: A voice can turn up just before a corner gets cut. A grandmother's, a coach's, a teacher who believed in someone. That person might not have been seen in years.
They might not be alive. But in certain moments they're right there, and it's easier to stand a little straighter. Marcus had an old rule for exactly that.
He'd found it written down somewhere, and copied it into book eleven.

teach.h: KEEP A GOOD PERSON IN MIND.

teach.b: In the writings of the Ephesians, Marcus says, there was this precept: keep constantly in mind one of the people of the past who lived with virtue. That's the whole entry. Second, a puzzle about the source.
Who were these Ephesians? Nobody is sure. Some editors have suggested it should read Epicureans, followers of Epicurus, and there's a reason to think so.
Seneca, in his eleventh letter, passes on Epicurus's advice: choose some good person and keep them always before your eyes, living as if they were watching.
Either way, Marcus says plainly that the rule wasn't his own; he copied it. Third, Marcus did it himself.
Book one of the Meditations reads like this practice.
It's a list of people and what he learned from each: his grandfather's good temper, his mother's generosity and simple way of living, his teachers, his adoptive father Antoninus.
Before the hard thinking begins, Marcus stops to remember good people, one by one, and what each gave him. Fourth, why it works. A rule is abstract.
A person is concrete. In a hard moment, what's right? is a big question.
What would she do? often answers itself.
The person you remember doesn't have to have been perfect. They only have to be good in the one way you need right now.

how: Some readers of the Meditations keep a particular person in mind, a grandparent, a teacher or a figure from history, and in hard moments ask what that person would do.

games.q: you're about to cut a corner. you're Marcus, with the old rule in mind. what do you do?
o: call to mind someone who lived with virtue.
games.why: keep in mind one of the people of the past who practiced virtue, says the rule he copied. Seneca credits Epicurus with similar advice: live as if a good person were watching.

practice: Bring one good person to mind, living or gone, well-known or known only to you, and remember one specific moment that showed who they were: the words they used, where you were standing.
If gratitude comes, let it, and let them stand beside you for a while.

carryVoice: Your line: remember them. Book one shows Marcus doing it, name by name. Until tomorrow.
